episodes.title: GPs, LPs, and the anatomy of a PE fund
takeaways: A PE fund is typically a limited partnership: LPs supply capital passively and are liable only up to their commitment, while the GP makes the decisions and carries legal responsibility.
Capital is committed up front but called only as needed, and the closed-end fund runs about ten years, so your sponsor's behavior is shaped by where the fund sits in its life.
Your sponsor answers to LPs and reports valuations to them, and lenders lend to your company, not the fund, so understanding the fund helps you read board, lender, and capital-allocation decisions.

episodes.title: Fund economics: management fees, hurdle rates, carry, and the waterfall
takeaways: The management fee, often about two percent, pays the GP firm to operate and is usually charged on committed capital early on; the real upside is carry, typically twenty percent of profit, paid only after LPs clear a hurdle, often eight percent compounded.

In a waterfall, cash flows in order: return of capital, preferred return, GP catch-up, then an eighty-twenty split; whole-fund and deal-by-deal versions change when the GP gets paid and how much risk it has an incentive to take.

For an operating executive, carry is earned at exit, so timing, EBITDA quality, and clean numbers matter. Sponsor fees paid by your company are watched and capped by lenders, and the sponsor reads your results against the whole fund.

episodes.title: The fund lifecycle and why the clock drives every decision
takeaways: A PE fund runs about ten years: roughly five years of investing, then a harvest period focused on exits, with possible extensions. Fees step down as it ages, so carry and realized cash matter more.

Time changes returns: the same 2.5 times money multiple is about a 20 percent IRR over five years but only about 14 percent over seven, and LPs judge the GP by cash returned (DPI) when it raises the next fund.

Know where your sponsor's fund is in its life, present initiatives with a timing case that shows payback before the likely exit window, and start legal, compliance, and retention readiness well before a sale.

episodes.title: The three return levers: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and deleveraging
takeaways: Sponsor returns come from three levers: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and debt paydown. EBITDA growth is the most controllable, deleveraging depends on cash conversion, and multiple expansion is the least controllable, so disciplined sponsors treat it as a bonus rather than a plan.

In the example, ten million dollars of added EBITDA at a ten times multiple created one hundred million dollars of value, thirty million of debt repayment added thirty million more, and a one-turn swing in the exit multiple moved the result by thirty million either way.

Executives should show that EBITDA is high quality and backed by cash, including working capital in a brokerage, and tie each initiative to a timing case, because buyers discount low-quality earnings and lenders are repaid with cash, not EBITDA.

episodes.title: IRR versus MOIC, and why sponsors watch both
takeaways: MOIC measures how many dollars come back per dollar invested but ignores time, while IRR is the annualized return that rewards getting cash back sooner, so sponsors watch both to judge size and speed.
The same multiple produces a lower IRR the longer the hold, and early distributions like dividend recaps raise IRR without changing MOIC, which is why timing and lender consent matter.

Executives should show payback timing for each initiative, understand that lenders care about cash and leverage rather than sponsor returns, and read management equity plans closely for how MOIC and IRR hurdles are defined.

episodes.title: EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, and the add-backs that get challenged
takeaways: EBITDA is a convention, not a GAAP measure, so adjusted EBITDA is only as good as the add-backs behind it. Buyers, lenders, and the board each test them differently, and buyers do it through a quality of earnings review.

Add-backs survive when they are truly non-recurring, documented, measurable, and applied consistently. Recurring "one-time" items, blended startup branch costs, and unrealized run-rate savings are the ones most often cut.

A gap between management's number and the diligenced number is multiplied by the exit multiple, so a five million dollar cut at ten times costs fifty million in value. Track one-time items as they happen, keep one reconciled bridge across all versions of EBITDA, and show how EBITDA converts to cash.

episodes.title: Reading the three financial statements like a sponsor
takeaways: Sponsors read the statements in a particular order: cash flow first, then the balance sheet to explain the gap between profit and cash, then the income statement to test the earnings story.

In a growing freight brokerage, receivables can grow faster than carrier payables, so strong EBITDA can still produce little free cash, as in the example where eight million dollars of EBITDA became one million.

Be ready to explain every large balance sheet and cash movement, and keep the statements, board reports, and lender definitions reconciled, because covenant calculations follow the credit agreement rather than GAAP.
